en.content:
Hong Kong’s rapid uptake of artificial intelligence, as reflected in today’s survey that finds over 90% of organisations have already adopted AI tools, is a telling sign of how quickly the city is positioning itself for a more data-driven economy. Yet the same survey also points to obvious gaps: many users appear to be moving faster than their training, internal safeguards, and policy frameworks. For a place that prides itself on rule-based governance and high standards in education, finance, and public services, “use first, govern later” may generate short-term efficiency while quietly raising longer-term risks.

This is not only a technical issue but also a social one. When schools, NGOs, and businesses deploy AI without consistent training, staff can misunderstand limitations, over-trust outputs, or fail to recognise when human oversight is essential. Different sectors face different sensitivities—an AI system shaping admissions decisions is not the same as one optimising an internal workflow. In Hong Kong’s context, where public confidence depends on clarity and accountability, even well-intentioned experimentation must be matched by practical guidance: how data is handled, how errors are corrected, and what “approval” means in real operational terms.

At the same time, adoption need not be framed as a purely defensive posture. Done well, AI can support Hong Kong’s broader development goals—enhancing productivity, improving service responsiveness, and widening access to assistance in education and community work. The key is to turn widespread use into responsible use. That means prioritising structured training for frontline users, creating clear internal policies on acceptable use, and establishing sector-specific risk assessments. Government can play a coordination role—supporting capacity-building and encouraging common standards—without stifling the city’s entrepreneurial dynamism.

Ultimately, the most significant challenge highlighted by the survey is not that organisations are adopting AI, but that their “readiness” may not yet match their “deployment.” If Hong Kong wants AI to become a durable advantage rather than a source of avoidable controversy, it should treat governance as part of implementation from the start. A pragmatic pathway—skills first, safeguards second, continuous review always—will better protect people, sustain trust, and allow the city to capture the benefits of AI in a manner consistent with its governance ethos.
en.topic_title: Over 90% of Hong Kong organisations use AI tools despite training and policy gaps, survey finds

zh.content:
今日最值得留意嘅主題係：本港超過九成機構已經「落地」使用AI，但同時培訓與政策出現明顯缺口。呢個訊號一方面反映業界同教育界追求效率、希望用AI減省人手與提升決策；但另一方面亦提醒我哋，技術嘅普及唔等於治理到位。當大量組織同時「開工」，如果缺乏清晰嘅資料保護、風險評估、採購與使用指引，AI便可能由工具變成放大器——放大錯誤、偏見，甚至洩露敏感資料。

更關鍵在於，現時多數討論只停留喺「有冇用」同「用咗幾多」，但社會更應追問：用咗之後責任由邊個負？結果有冇可追溯性？涉及個人資料、學生學習數據、醫療或福利等範疇時，當演算法出錯、或出現歧視性輸出，機構係點樣補救、點樣向受影響者交代？如果唔先建立制度性嘅制衡，AI嘅部署就會變成「先上車、後補票」，令合規成本喺出事後才集中爆發。

我哋嘅立場係：面對AI滲透得咁快，政府與監管部門唔應只做宣傳或口號，而要加快落實可操作嘅指引框架，令機構知道「邊類任務可以用、邊類資料唔可以用、出現事故點樣通報」。同時，機構亦要自我要求——唔好只靠技術供應商提供模板就算，而係要投資於員工培訓、建立內部審批與抽查機制，並設定明確嘅人手覆核流程。教育界更要把AI素養「變成課程與考核」而唔係只係工具推介，讓學生理解AI局限與資訊辨識能力。

AI在本港已經進入「普及期」，爭議唔係在於要唔要用，而係用得有冇規矩、用得有冇底線。要令呢波科技轉型真正轉化為生產力與公共服務改善，就必須同步補齊政策與培訓缺口；否則，效率嘅得益可能會被風險嘅代價抵消，甚至削弱市民對制度與決策透明度嘅信心。
